opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think we're in this really interesting middle phase. A couple of years ago, computer use was mostly a demo: you'd watch a model slowly click around a browser, and it was impressive that it worked at all. Now the models have gotten much better at the core perception and action loop. They can read a screen, understand what UI elements do, and take reasonable next steps. For short, well-scoped tasks, like filling out a form, pulling information from a few tabs, or navigating a settings page, they're genuinely useful.

Where they still struggle is long-horizon reliability. If a task has twenty or thirty steps, small errors compound. The agent misreads a dropdown, or it doesn't notice that a page didn't load, and then it confidently keeps going down the wrong path. Humans are very good at noticing when something feels off and backing up. Models are getting better at that kind of self-correction, but it's not yet robust.

The other big piece is trust and the human-in-the-loop design. I think a lot of the product work right now is figuring out when the agent should just act and when it should check in. If it asks too often, it's annoying and you might as well do it yourself. If it asks too rarely, you get anxious about it buying the wrong thing or sending the wrong email. Getting that calibration right matters as much as raw capability.

So my overall assessment is that the capability curve is steep, and the bottleneck is shifting from "can the model do this at all" to "can it do this reliably, safely, and in a way people actually want to delegate to." That's a much more exciting problem to be working on, because it means we're close to real everyday usefulness.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're in this interesting in-between phase. If you look at the benchmarks, OSWorld and things like that, the numbers have climbed a lot in the last couple of years, and the models can now genuinely navigate a browser, fill out forms, move between apps, recover from a lot of small failures. That part is real. But if you actually sit and watch an agent work on a long task, you still see the gap between "can do it in a demo" and "I'd let it run unsupervised on my actual accounts."

A few things stand out to me. The first is that the hard part was never clicking the right pixel. It's maintaining state over a long horizon. Twenty steps in, the agent has to remember why it opened that tab, what it already tried, and what the user actually cares about, and that's where things still drift. The second is that the environment is adversarial in a boring way. Pop-ups, login walls, layouts that change, latency. Humans just absorb that friction without thinking, and models are only now getting robust to it. And the third is calibration. The best agents today know when to stop and ask instead of confidently doing the wrong thing, and I actually think that's a bigger unlock than raw capability, because it's what makes people willing to delegate.

So my honest assessment is that computer use is past the toy stage but not yet at the "it just works" stage. The trajectory is steep, though. A lot of what felt impossible eighteen months ago is now routine, and I'd expect the bottleneck to shift from "can the model do it" toward "how do we give it safe, well-scoped access to the things it needs" over the next year.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re at an interesting stage where agents can do useful things on a computer, but reliability is still the central challenge. There’s a big difference between completing a task once in a demo and completing it consistently when the interface changes or something unexpected happens.

I’d look at how much intervention they need, whether they can recognize a mistake, and whether they can recover. If you have to watch every click, you’re still doing a lot of the work. The meaningful milestone is being able to delegate a task and trust the agent to finish it—or tell you clearly where it got stuck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re at an exciting but still early stage. Computer-use agents can complete useful tasks, but there’s a big gap between a compelling demo and something you can reliably delegate work to. A task might involve dozens of steps, and small errors compound along the way.

So I’d assess them less by whether they can click the right button and more by whether they can recognize a mistake, recover, and know when to ask for help. The interesting threshold is when you can give an agent an outcome you want, walk away, and trust that it will either finish or explain clearly what blocked it.
